Latest Update: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post reveals a pattern that meets both requirements.
  • Sources indicate that we built and tested the pattern in the US East (N.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions. Agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, must meet the same two requirements. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model.

Recent findings suggest that this post reveals a pattern that meets both requirements. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions. It covers where to place the Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway that the Gateway uses to reach private targets. It also covers who owns each piece, six configuration decisions, and the checks that confirm the pattern works.

Sources indicate that we built and tested the pattern in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1), in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are in the companion repository. Use the pattern as a guideline and adjust it to your own account architecture.

Use this pattern when all of the following are true:.

Otherwise, one of the options in Table 1 fits better.

Table 1: When another option fits better.

Recent findings suggest that we also considered managed mode in subnets that AgentCore owns, a resource gateway in each tool VPC or in the central endpoints VPC, and internet-facing load balancers with AWS WAF per tool. The alternatives write-up explains why each falls short under these constraints.

AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through a VPC Lattice resource gateway, and the two private endpoint modes place it differently. Managed mode creates it in the Gateway account, which fits environments where that account can own the subnets it runs in. Self-managed mode, as documented, places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, which fits environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool. This environment needs both conditions at once, so the pattern uses self-managed mode with one change. The network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway, so every request and reply passes the inspection VPC.

Give the resource gateway its own VPC and subnets in the network account. Don’t share them, and keep backends out of them. Route them through the transit gateway so every request and reply between VPCs crosses the firewall. Share one resource configuration per backend with the AgentCore account through AWS RAM. Figure 1 highlights the accounts, VPCs, and traffic path.

Figure 1: The network account owns every VPC and the resource gateway. The other accounts own only what they place in shared subnets. Solid lines cross the firewall in both directions. Step numbers match the following traffic path.

How does Gateway traffic enter the network account’s VPC without a transit gateway attachment in the AgentCore account? When you create a target, AgentCore associates the shared resource configuration with its own VPC Lattice service network. VPC Lattice then delivers connections from that service network to the resource gateway’s network interfaces in your VPC. AWS operates that hop, and from there your routes and firewall take over.

What this pattern doesn’t do. Check these limits against your requirements before you adopt it:.

Sources indicate that A new operation or tool on an existing target needs no new target: update the OpenAPI spec with UpdateGatewayTarget, or call SynchronizeGatewayTargets for an MCP server. The repository’s build order lists the steps in each account and the values the teams pass to each other.

The snippets are excerpts from the lab templates and use the lab’s address initiative. RGW_NET is the resource gateway subnets (10.0.1.0/24–10.0.3.0/24), TOOL_NET is the tool VPC (10.12.0.0/16), and ALB_NET is the ALB subnets in it.

Create a dedicated VPC in the network account for the resource gateway, with subnets you don’t share and no central endpoints or backends. Route those subnets to the transit gateway. Keep one resource gateway per trust zone.

Used only with AgentCore, the resource gateway consumes one IP address per subnet, so small subnets are enough. Two settings can’t be changed after creation, Ipv4AddressesPerEni and ResourceConfigDnsResolution, so choose them up front. Use Availability Zone IDs that VPC Lattice and your AgentCore features support. The lab layout lists them for us-east-1.

According to recent reports, point the resource configuration at the internal ALB DNS name and share it with the AgentCore account. Don’t start the name with rcfg-, which VPC Lattice reserves.

VPC Lattice delivers the connection to the resource configuration’s domain. AgentCore sends the target URL’s host name (for example tools.example.internal) as the SNI and checks the ALB certificate against it. The certificate’s subject alternative name must match that host name. The host name doesn’t need to resolve in DNS.

For private API Gateway REST APIs, point one resource configuration at the network account’s execute-api interface endpoint. Each API’s target uses its own URL, and each API’s resource policy must allow that endpoint through aws:SourceVpce. In our tests, a second API in another account worked through the same resource configuration with no network change.

Industry observers note that your firewall needs two stateful allows: from the resource gateway subnets to the tool VPC on port 443, and from the ALB subnets to the identity provider’s host name on port 443. Session-based firewalls pass replies of an allowed flow. In the lab we used AWS Network Firewall with strict rule order and the default actions Drop established and Alert established. With these defaults, the firewall drops client-to-server packets that no rule passes, and lets replies through unless a rule drops them. The rule-order notes explain the semantics.

In a recent development, the first rule allows only the resource gateway subnets to reach the tool VPC on port 443. The second allows the ALB to fetch its identity provider’s signing keys (JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS), only from the ALB subnets and only to the identity provider’s host name. The tool VPC needs a default route to the transit gateway for this fetch to reach central egress. If your identity provider isn’t Amazon Cognito, replace the host name. Without this rule, in our tests, the ALB returned HTTP 500 and the agent received MCP invocation failed.

To prove replies cross the firewall, we added a drop rule for the reply direction preceding the pass rule:.

In a recent development, tool calls then hung until timeout, and the firewall logged to_client drops for sid 100098. Removing the rule restored the calls. Run the same test on your own firewall.

The tool account keeps its own identity provider (Amazon Cognito in the lab) and creates an app client for the Gateway. Validate that client’s token on every path to the backend.

Sources indicate that internal ALB – Make the listener’s default action a fixed response, and put a jwt-validation action on every rule that forwards. Pin client_id to the Gateway’s app client so that other clients in the same user pool are rejected.

In our tests, a target with no token, one with another identity provider’s token, and one with a different app client’s token were all rejected with HTTP 401 before the backend ran. The agent saw only An internal error occurred, so use the ALB access logs to diagnose token problems.

In a recent development, private REST API – An API key doesn’t authenticate the caller, so add an authorizer to every method, such as a Cognito user pool authorizer with a required scope (as in the lab). Also attach an endpoint policy to the execute-api endpoint that limits it to APIs owned by approved accounts. It controls which APIs the endpoint reaches, not who calls it. The authorizer controls the caller.

The ALB or endpoint security group allows only the resource gateway subnets, so the resource gateway is the only network path in. If your firewall applies source NAT, the security group must allow the firewall’s addresses instead, and it then admits anything the firewall forwards. The firewall rule and the token validation become the controls.

Create the Gateway with a JWT authorizer and, optionally, an AWS WAF web access control list (web ACL), which inspects the tool-call arguments for every target. AWS WAF inspects only the first 16 KB of the body by default (adjustable to 64 KB), so decide how each rule handles larger bodies. Add AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to the common rule set. See the AWS WAF notes.

Gateway targets with a private endpoint can’t use NO_AUTH for inbound authorization unless you configure an interceptor function.

Each target needs an OAuth credential provider that holds the tool account’s app client ID and secret and the identity provider’s discovery URL:.

If the ALB uses a certificate from a private certificate authority (CA), also store the CA certificate as a PEM string in an AWS Secrets Manager secret. The Gateway execution role (the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role you give the Gateway when you create it) needs permission to read that secret and the credential provider.

It has been revealed that an OpenAPI target uses the same blocks with openApiSchema in place of mcpServer. To rotate the CA, patch the secret and call UpdateGatewayTarget. Open connections can keep the old trust material for up to 15 minutes.

In a recent development, keep the Gateway the only consumer of the shared resource configuration. The AWS managed permission for AWS RAM also grants ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint, so the AgentCore account could reach the backend through a resource VPC endpoint or service network of its own. A customer managed permission can’t fix this: AWS RAM rejects vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService in one, and without it Gateway targets fail. Attach an SCP to the AgentCore account instead:.

With this SCP, our attempts to create a resource VPC endpoint and a service network association of its own were denied, and a new Gateway target still reached READY. SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so don’t run AgentCore there. In the network account, alarm on unexpected associations with an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the AWS CloudTrail event CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociationBySharee.

Revoke access by deleting the Gateway targets (or the service network resource association) first, then removing the resource configuration from the share. Removing it from the share alone doesn’t remove existing associations.

Create the Gateway interface endpoint in the shared agent VPC with private DNS enabled, and attach an endpoint policy that lists the approved Gateways. The principal must be *, because the Gateway authenticates callers with bearer tokens. The Resource list is the control.

In our tests, a second Gateway called through the same endpoint returned JSON-RPC error -32002 Insufficient permissions, but still answered on its public endpoint.

Recent findings suggest that the interface endpoint doesn’t close the Gateway’s public endpoint. Attach a resource policy that allows bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway only when aws:SourceVpce is your endpoint and denies it otherwise (the full policy is in the repository). In our tests, internet calls returned -32002 about 30 seconds after we applied it, while endpoint calls kept working. AWS notes policy changes can take up to 15 minutes.

According to recent reports, an agent with no internet route still needs its inbound JWT. Give it a path to its identity provider’s token endpoint, such as a route to the transit gateway and a firewall rule scoped like the JWKS rule in Decision 3. Alternatively, use a private identity provider.

Recent findings suggest that before you rely on the pattern, run these checks in a non-production copy of your network account, with your own firewall. The full list of 14 checks, with how to run each and the results we saw, is in the repository, along with a log source for every hop.

If a check fails or the agent gets a generic error, the troubleshooting guide maps each symptom to the log that shows the cause.

When your network team owns every subnet and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall, place the VPC Lattice resource gateway in the network account and route its subnets through the transit gateway. The network team sets up the entry point once and adds one resource configuration per backend load balancer. Application teams keep owning only their load balancers, security groups, identity providers, and Gateway targets, and AWS WAF moves from per-tool public load balancers to the Gateway. Run the validation checks in your own environment before you rely on the pattern.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

Sources indicate that stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. He also received the Federal CIO Council Leadership award for related work.

Industry observers note that prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

It has been revealed that view CSAF Summary Siemens is currently assessing the impact of Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) on Industrial Edge. Please check your Industrial Edge Management (IEM) setup: - No Management Applications installed: No action is required. Although the affected Brotli library is included in the IEM software stack, the affected functionality is not used or exposed. The same applies to IEDK. - Management Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. - Device Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. For Siemens-managed services, Industrial Edge Hub and Industrial Edge Management Cloud, appropriate Firewall/WAF protection has already been implemented. Siemens has released latest versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge Management are affected: Cloud Connector Configurator vers:intdot/<1.24.3 (CVE-2026-111497) Common Configurator (CC on IEM) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) Common Configurator on Device (CC on Edge) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) Data Flow Monitoring vers:intdot/<3.0.18 (CVE-2026-111497) Databus Configurator vers:intdot/<4.0.1 (CVE-2026-111497) DataXess Configurator vers:intdot/<1.5.7 (CVE-2026-111497) Edge OPC UA Server Configurator vers:intdot/<2.3.10 (CVE-2026-111497) Flow Creator Configurator vers:intdot/<1.15.1 (CVE-2026-111497) Industrial Edge Hub vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) Industrial Edge Management Cloud vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Siemens Cloud Connector Configurator 1 Vulnerability Out-of-bounds Write Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Firm Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-111497 A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Owners need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends configuring the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Sources indicate that during the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly notable in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Sources indicate that today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

According to recent reports, we are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-people. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

Industry observers note that the project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

According to recent reports, to reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

In a recent development, the underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the presently implemented backends can be found here.

In a recent development, we are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#2346. How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2247 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department.
  • Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications.
  • Sources indicate that semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department.

Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications. Most campaigns begin with the same video discovery problem: finding the one moment in the footage that will resonate with an audience. When a brief lands, the clock starts, and what they need is almost never something a database can describe.

Sources indicate that semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate. Ask it for a character holding a coffee mug and it will find every coffee mug in a thousand episodes. The queries that actually drive entertainment campaigns look nothing like that. They are questions of judgment: which moment in a show will travel, which line is quotable, and which single frame will work as a meme.

Those questions can’t be typed into a search box. Answering them requires two things the search index doesn’t have: an editorial definition of what “quotable” or “memeable” means for a given library, and a continuously refreshed view of what is moving outside the library. Historically, answering them meant a person with deep knowledge of the show watching footage for a week, and that person doesn’t scale across a catalog.

In this post, we describe how Social Department, the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, set out to encode those editorial questions as executable retrieval pipelines. The result is QuickSearch, a set of single-action queries that return the clips a marketer is looking for without requiring them to describe it: Shareable Scenes, Quotable Quotes, Memeable Moments, and Trend Align.

The models in this solution run on Amazon Bedrock, so customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. It isn’t shared with model providers and isn’t used to train the underlying models.

Social Department’s approach to responsible AI is that AI proposes and people decide. In production, code checks generated output against the source material (for example, a quote is discarded if it isn’t in the episode transcript). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen customer search text for prompt attacks, and a person on the customer’s team approves every post before it publishes.

Industry observers note that social Department owns the pipeline architecture, the retrieval system, and the editorial criteria behind each action. TrackIt, an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner, implemented and delivered against that design. TwelveLabs’ Marengo 3.0 and Pegasus 1.2 models on Amazon Bedrock provide the scene-level video reasoning the pipeline builds on. AWS supplies the infrastructure, the model access including Anthropic’s Claude models, and Amazon OpenSearch Service, using its serverless option, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, for retrieval.

A note on scope: This post describes the AWS portions of the system: the ingest and indexing pipeline, the retrieval path, and the services that run them. The components Social Department owns, including its media and data backbone, content analysis and discovery engine, editorial criteria, and evaluation program, are described only to the depth needed to follow the architecture. The named services that follow are the ones this post is about, not an inventory of Social Department’s full system.

Industry observers note that social Department is the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, serving major studios, networks, streamers, and FAST applications. It automates campaign strategy, asset creation, publishing, and performance optimization across a client’s full content library. Most of those functions depend on locating the right moment inside the footage first, and semantic clip discovery has been core to the product from the beginning.

Entertainment marketing operates under two constraints that a general-purpose search layer can’t satisfy.

A marketer can describe an object, a location, or a line of dialogue, but not what will travel. That judgment, this moment lands and that one doesn’t, is the actual skill in the job. It was never automatable because it depends on knowing how an audience behaves rather than what a video contains. A search layer that only understands content requires a human to supply the intent, and supplying that intent well requires having already watched the show.

No amount of video understanding tells you what audiences are talking about this morning. That information is created outside the library and changes hourly, while a library changes only when latest content is added. A system that answers these queries has to acquire trend signal continuously and reconcile it against the library at request time.

That distinction drove the core architectural decision: content understanding and trend acquisition run as independent pipelines on their own schedules and are joined only when a user selects a QuickSearch action.

In a recent development, with QuickSearch, teams can interact with a video library in a different way, one where the system proposes rather than waits. It provides four actions, each with its own retrieval strategy, editorial criteria, and ranking model. The walkthrough that follows describes how each is implemented. The list here introduces what they do.

Alongside these, Social Department keeps natural-language search for everything the actions don’t cover, and image-based search, where a reference image returns visually similar content across the library.

Industry observers note that the following diagram shows how the three parts of the architecture connect. The content understanding pipeline makes the library searchable, and the trend acquisition lanes pull in external trend signal. The QuickSearch job layer joins the two at request time.

Figure 1: High-level architecture.

According to recent reports, the system has three parts that run on independent schedules. Two acquire and structure information. The third resolves a user’s single selection into a multi-stage retrieval operation across both.

This pipeline makes the library legible. It works asynchronously on ingest. An AWS Step Functions state machine orchestrates roughly two dozen Python AWS Lambda functions end to end. The following steps trace one video from upload to indexed clips.

In a recent development, the pipeline is event-driven end to end. Every Lambda task retries with exponential backoff. The scene-description stage adds a dedicated throttling retry with full jitter. Non-critical enrichment steps degrade gracefully rather than failing the run, and a hard failure routes to an error handler that records the reason and reports the asset as failed.

In a recent development, same-Region staging for Marengo. Marengo is available in a specific set of AWS Regions. Asynchronous invocation in Amazon Bedrock reads input from and writes output to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as the endpoint. The pipeline is built around those parameters. It stages each video into a dedicated bucket in US East (N. Virginia) before invoking Marengo, then reads the embedding output back from the same bucket. The rest of the infrastructure stays in its home Region while each embedding job runs alongside the model. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

This pipeline operates continuously and independently of any library, and it is what makes Trend Align possible.

Quotable Quotes draws on a second, narrower input: an external dialogue popularity signal, used strictly to weight lines that have already circulated. It’s optional by design, so if the signal is unavailable a line gets no boost rather than failing the job.

Sources indicate that this layer is where a single selection becomes a retrieval strategy. It executes each action asynchronously and returns a ranked set of clips.

Three choices made culturally informed retrieval tractable.

Recent findings suggest that A library changes when new content is added. Trends change daily, and early-stage trends faster than that. Coupling the two would mean either reprocessing content against fresh signal, which is computationally untenable, or serving stale trend judgment. Keeping them as independent pipelines joined at request time means signal stays current without the library ever being touched again. A title that finished airing years ago can re-enter a live conversation.

Recent findings suggest that the naive design puts one large model in front of the whole library. QuickSearch instead uses inexpensive, high-recall vector and keyword retrieval to build a candidate pool, then spends model budget only on ranking a capped set of real candidates. The caps are sized against the ranking model’s output token limit, because a ranker that truncates mid-response silently drops results. This also keeps the per-query cost of Amazon Bedrock predictable: one embedding call, one rerank call, and a small fixed number of Claude invocations, regardless of library size.

Results are cached for 30 days. Without intervention, a change to an action’s criteria or model would stay invisible to owners until the cache expired. Each action carries a pipeline version that is bumped in the same change that alters its behavior. That bump invalidates prior results immediately, so editorial judgment is refined as a versioned change to the product rather than relitigated on every query.

Industry observers note that social Department reports the following outcomes from customer use of QuickSearch. These are the company’s own observations rather than a controlled benchmark.

“The hard part here was never the search. It was working out what to search for: how you take something a great marketer does on instinct, about which moment lands and why, and turn it into criteria a system can execute a thousand times. We spent a long time on that. Working with TrackIt on a compressed timeline, we went from spec to a live demo at NAB. TwelveLabs gives us the intelligence to understand what’s inside the footage and AWS gives us the infrastructure to do it at library scale. Our job is to know what to point it at.”.

— Jonathan Verk, Founder and CEO, Social Department.

In a recent development, “Everyone in media talks about adding metadata to their libraries but tagging content doesn’t pay for itself. What I like about this project is that it closes the loop. It takes highlights sitting in an archive and makes them useful for real campaigns, at a cost that makes sense to run every day. That’s the part the industry has been missing.”.

— Chris Marchitelli, Vice President, TrackIt.

The following four lessons from the project stood out.

In a recent development, retrieval is largely solved. What isn’t solved is specifying intent precisely enough for retrieval to be useful without an expert marketer in the loop. Most of the engineering effort went into defining what qualifies as a shareable scene or a memeable frame, tightly enough to execute repeatedly across libraries with different tones and audiences. That definition is the output of a standing evaluation program of numbered iterations, each measured against per-show ground-truth sets and a tracked baseline, that tunes the criteria against results rather than intuition.

QuickSearch uses a multi-model architecture, with each model assigned to the work it fits best. Claude Haiku handles bounded, cost-sensitive output, and Claude Sonnet handles tasks where cultural recall changes the answer. TwelveLabs Marengo produces multimodal embeddings, TwelveLabs Pegasus provides scene-level video reasoning, and the Amazon Rerank model handles reranking. Amazon Bedrock made this architecture practical to build and run. Models from TwelveLabs, Anthropic, and Amazon are available through one API, so Social Department can change the model behind a task when measured quality moves, without building a new integration. Asynchronous invocation runs long video embedding jobs at library scale, and the Rerank API adds a relevance pass without separately hosted infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen search input in the same service, and customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. Because Amazon Bedrock is fully managed, the team operates no model-serving infrastructure of its own.

Treating trend data as another input to the content pipeline would have failed, because the two have incompatible lifecycles. Recognizing early that library content and live culture are separate systems, with separate refresh rates, storage, and failure modes, was the decision the rest of the design depended on.

According to recent reports, social Department owned the pipeline architecture, retrieval system, and editorial criteria. TrackIt built and delivered against that architecture, and TwelveLabs supplied the video understanding models. AWS, with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, provided the infrastructure, model access, and solution architecture for the AWS components. Because each party had a clearly defined scope, the 8-week production timeline held.

In a recent development, we described how Social Department, working with TrackIt, TwelveLabs, and AWS, built culture-aware video discovery for entertainment marketing using its own pipeline and retrieval architecture. Several AWS components make up the layer this post describes. TwelveLabs Marengo handles multimodal embedding and TwelveLabs Pegasus handles scene-level video reasoning, both on Amazon Bedrock. Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock handle interpretation and editorial ranking, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless handles hybrid retrieval. AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, AWS Elemental MediaConvert, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon SQS run the pipelines around them. The result is a set of single-action queries that return the clips audiences already care about, the lines they already quote, the frames that will work as memes, and the moments that connect to whatever is trending right now.

To get started with multimodal video understanding on AWS, explore Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. To learn more about the TwelveLabs models available on Amazon Bedrock, visit the TwelveLabs page on AWS Marketplace. To explore how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help your organization, visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center page.

XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help consumers who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
  • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
  • Recent findings suggest that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help consumers who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Recent findings suggest that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

Recent findings suggest that people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when consumers don't know the right questions to ask.

Recent findings suggest that we built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

Sources indicate that A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

Recent findings suggest that to validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

In a recent development, we evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

In a recent development, A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

Recent findings suggest that we also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

Sources indicate that A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Recent findings suggest that researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to consumers’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

According to recent reports, future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what customers need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench right now covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

  • This post demonstrates how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.

It has been revealed that salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem.

This post demonstrates how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed.

According to recent reports, salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet promptly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out.

Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic.

Industry observers note that building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path.

Industry observers note that the inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components.

Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it.

According to recent reports, the router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of latest requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance launches affect how promptly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination.

Industry observers note that client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows.

Recent findings suggest that in Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct InvokeEndpoint call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code.

Figure 1: End-to-end architecture for cross-Region inference routing at Salesforce. In each Region, the Internal Gateway sends client requests through a VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink). Requests with the data residency flag set to true go directly to the in-Region Endpoint A and never leave their Region. All other requests go to the local inference router, which sends traffic to its local Endpoint A by default and fails over to Endpoint A in another Region when the local endpoint shows signs of capacity constraints.

Industry observers note that salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line highlights whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift.

Recent findings suggest that the gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident.

The following walkthrough indicates the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.

Sources indicate that in the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, with a condition that limits access to one named router. The router does not need to exist yet, so you can use the ARN of the router you strategy to create.

Industry observers note that the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition means the router account can reach the endpoint only through that router. The endpoint owner can revoke access at any time with delete-endpoint-policy.

In the router account, create the router in us-west-2 with one routing target that lists both destinations by ARN.

Each additional model becomes another entry in RoutingTargets.

Recent findings suggest that before sending traffic, call DescribeInferenceRouter and check each destination’s RoutingStatus. Routable means SageMaker AI could read the destination and it can serve traffic. Unroutable means the destination was read but can’t serve right now, for example because the endpoint is not InService. Unknown means SageMaker AI couldn’t read the destination with your credentials, for example because you lack sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint (or sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent for an inference component), or, for a destination in another account, because its endpoint policy doesn’t grant Describe.

In a recent development, the change in the calling code is small. The request body, content type, and accept type stay exactly as they were. The client and operation change, and the endpoint name is replaced by the router name and the routing target name.

An InferenceId and CustomAttributes are passed through to the destination as with InvokeEndpoint, so identifiers such as a trace ID travel with the request. Members such as TargetVariant and InferenceComponentName are not used, because the routing target replaces them.

Most teams evaluating a routing layer first ask how to tell what it did. The inference router answers on every response and in Amazon CloudWatch. Each response carries the ARN of the destination that served it and a routing reason, in the InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields and in the matching X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routed-Resource-Arn and X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routing-Reason headers. Because the ARN includes the Region and account, logging both values with your own request logs gives you a per-request record of whether each call ran locally or crossed a boundary.

The routing reason takes one of four values. local-preferred means a healthy destination in the router’s Region served the request. failover means a destination in the router’s Region exists but isn’t serving reliably, so the router sent the request elsewhere. capacity-available means no destination in the router’s Region could take the request, and it went to one of several healthy destinations in other Regions. only-healthy means it was served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.

It has been revealed that in aggregate, the router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, each carrying the router name and destination ARN, so the cross-Region picture is visible from one place. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations counts requests per destination, and its error.type attribute splits failures into invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx (including timeouts), and invocation_model_error for errors returned by the model.

Sources indicate that aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration measures the time each destination took, and aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration measures the time the router added, including the network to and from a remote Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status reports each destination’s health state as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. You query these metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch Query Studio, and you can place them next to each endpoint’s existing SageMaker AI metrics on a cross-account, cross-Region dashboard.

Figure 2: CloudWatch dashboard during a failover test run by AWS with a test model. Requests per destination shift from the local us-east-2 endpoint to endpoints in us-west-2 as the local destination becomes degraded, then return gradually after recovery.

Salesforce tested the router in two configurations. First, same-Region routing in us-west-2, where the Internal Gateway called the local inference router and the router sent requests to the local Endpoint A. Second, cross-account, cross-Region routing, where the router in us-west-2 also listed an endpoint in us-east-2 owned by a separate infrastructure account. Before sending traffic, the team called DescribeInferenceRouter and confirmed that the routing target listed both destinations and that both reported a RoutingStatus of Routable. Requests sent to the router were then served by the local endpoint, with a routing reason of local-preferred. Setup took little effort: the endpoint owner added an endpoint policy for the router’s account, and the router call replaced the direct InvokeEndpoint call in the gateway’s egress path, with the same request body, content type, and accept type.

To test failover, the team flooded the local endpoint in us-west-2 until it was saturated, while a separate probe kept invoking the router and recorded where each request was served and how long it took. For about five minutes of saturation, probe latency at p50 rose from 0.2 seconds to 45 to 58 seconds, and traffic stayed in us-west-2. This is the intended behavior, because latency alone does not move traffic. When requests began to exceed the model container’s 60-second handler timeout and return errors, the router started to shift traffic. The first requests reached us-east-2 about two minutes after the first errors, and within another minute about 78 percent of probe traffic was served in us-east-2. The remaining 20 to 25 percent stayed local so the router could detect recovery.

Once traffic had moved, p50 latency returned to 0.2 seconds, and the cross-Region path added under 100 milliseconds at p50. After the local endpoint recovered, traffic returned to us-west-2 gradually over about 10 minutes, and the probe recorded no errors during failover or failback. The InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields on each response, together with the router’s per-destination invocation metrics in CloudWatch, showed the whole sequence without any extra instrumentation.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Share of probe requests by Region during the Salesforce failover test (UTC). Traffic stays in us-west-2 while the local endpoint is saturated, shifts to us-east-2 once requests begin returning errors (peaking at about 78 percent), then returns gradually to us-west-2 over about 10 minutes after recovery.

The router lets Salesforce replace operational logic the team used to build and run itself: the health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic in the Internal Gateway. Capacity signals and failover now live in the routing layer, not in each application.

Before broader adoption, Salesforce looks to repeat the failover test with the local endpoint held at saturation for longer, measure cross-Region latency at millisecond precision, evaluate cascading-Region behavior at the cross-Region cap, and roll out the router across more Regions.

“With the upcoming cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI, we can add capacity securely and keep our data residency commitments. Workloads that must stay in a region stay there, and only eligible traffic can be served from another Region. A single managed call works alongside our existing failover logic, so we didn’t have to re-architect our application or change our payloads. SageMaker AI handles routing, health detection, and fallback, and customer data always stays within the Salesforce trust boundary. We decide which Regions are eligible and control access through endpoint policies that we own. Because inference router works with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail, we also get a complete observability, cost-tracking, and governance architecture for our workloads.”.

— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce.

Keep the same model, container image, and artifacts available in every Region you register, because the router does not copy them, and a destination that runs a different model version will return different answers to the same request.

Size each destination Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you expect to send it. The router does not create capacity, and if every eligible destination is busy, your application receives the destinations’ own errors. Configure autoscaling on each destination the way you do today, with enough headroom that a receiving endpoint can scale out under its own policy when traffic arrives from another Region.

Customers can set the cap in the receiving endpoint’s configuration (CrossRegionTrafficConfig), as a per-instance request rate and the largest share of the endpoint’s capacity that remote traffic may use. Local traffic never counts against the cap. When remote traffic reaches it, the endpoint stops accepting additional requests from other Regions and the router sends them to other destinations, so local callers keep their capacity. The cap applies to real-time endpoints.

In a recent development, salesforce serves a wide variety of models for products across the organization in 30+ global Regions, and hosting them separately in each Region had turned capacity shortfalls into availability problems. With the inference router, Salesforce registers the endpoints it already runs in different Regions and accounts behind one call, so traffic that a local endpoint cannot serve reaches capacity elsewhere instead of failing. Requests that must stay in a Region stay there, endpoint owners authorize cross-account access through policies they control, and every response highlights where a request ran and why. SageMaker AI handles the routing, health assessment, and gradual return of traffic after recovery, instead of each calling application building that logic itself. This lets Salesforce add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.

It has been revealed that the cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI is generally available starting November 18, 2026, in all commercial Regions where inference is supported for real-time endpoints. To get started, see the Inference router documentation in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and the CreateInferenceRouter API reference.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

View CSAF Summary meta-iot2050 (https://github.com/siemens/meta-iot2050) from V01.03.01 contains a Command Injection vulnerability in the firmware patch tool that could allow an attacker which is able to manipulate a configuration file to have arbitrary commands run as root. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens meta-iot2050 are affected: meta-iot2050 vers:intdot/>=01.03.01 (CVE-2026-109830) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.3 Siemens meta-iot2050 1 Vulnerability Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Organization Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109830 Affected devices take parts from a configuration file and execute them unchecked. This could allow an attacker which is able to manipulate the configuration file to make the user execute arbitrary code on the device. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics.
