#2328. Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1997 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network.
  • AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers.
  • According to recent reports, in this post, we show you how to concern an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network. These IdPs usually present a TLS server certificate from a private certificate authority (CA). With private CA support in AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, your agents can now connect to these IdPs while trusting the private CA that your organization already uses.

AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers. You store the PEM-encoded CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference it from your credential provider. The CA certificate contains only the public certificate, not its private key. AgentCore Identity uses it to validate the server certificate presented by your IdP’s discovery, JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), and token endpoints. The CA certificate must be a root or intermediate CA certificate.

According to recent reports, in this post, we show you how to concern an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority. We then configure an AgentCore Identity credential provider to trust it and rotate the CA while minimizing downtime. We also show how to protect the CA certificate so that only your IdP team can change it. Although AgentCore Identity supports any private CA, including enterprise, third-party, and self-signed root CAs, the walkthrough in this post uses AWS Private CA and Keycloak as the IdP.

It has been revealed that consider an agent that needs to call an internal wiki API protected by your Keycloak IdP. The agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which hosts your agent code. To get an OAuth 2.0 access token from Keycloak, the agent uses an AgentCore Identity credential provider, which holds the IdP connection details and client credentials.

The following diagram reveals this setup. Keycloak runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The load balancer presents an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) private certificate signed by AWS Private CA. The CA certificate that AgentCore Identity trusts is stored in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.

AgentCore Identity reaches the IdP privately through Amazon VPC Lattice, which connects to your VPC through a resource gateway, an entry point for VPC Lattice traffic into your VPC. VPC Lattice is required for private CA support. If you choose the managed option, AgentCore Identity creates and manages the VPC Lattice resources for you.

Figure 1: Connecting AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a private CA.

Agents that use machine-to-machine, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated flows can also use the private CA without changing their code.

To follow this walkthrough, you need:.

Keep the following in mind when you plan your deployment:.

Recent findings suggest that the walkthrough has four steps. If your IdP already presents a certificate from your enterprise CA, skip to Step 2.

Start by creating a root CA in AWS Private CA. For instructions, see Create a private CA and Install the CA certificate. Choose general-purpose mode, because short-lived certificate mode issues certificates that are valid for 7 days or less. When you create the CA, authorize ACM to renew certificates, so that ACM can renew the IdP’s server certificate before it expires.

Sources indicate that next, request the server certificate. AgentCore Identity checks that the certificate matches the IdP hostname, so include each hostname that appears in your IdP’s discovery document as a subject alternative name (SAN). In most Keycloak deployments, the discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints share one hostname. For example, if your discovery URL is https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration, add keycloak.example.local as a SAN.

To request a private certificate for the IdP (console).

Industry observers note that agentCore Identity needs to trust the CA certificate to validate the IdP’s server certificate. Because it trusts the CA rather than the server certificate itself, you don’t need to update the credential provider each time the server certificate renews.

Export the CA certificate from AWS Private CA in PEM format:.

Before you upload the file, check it against the requirements. The file must be PEM-encoded and meet size requirements, containing only CA certificates that are within their validity period. The following commands show the CA flag, expiry date, and file size. The last command confirms that the IdP’s certificate chains to this CA. Run it from a host that can reach the IdP. It returns Verify return code: 0 (ok) when the chain is valid.

The output looks similar to the following:.

Recent findings suggest that store the file in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. A Secrets Manager secret must be a string secret in the same account as the credential provider. An S3 object can be in another account, which suits organizations that run the IdP in a central account.

Give write access to the secret or object only to the team that operates your IdP. For an example policy, see Protect the CA certificate later in this post.

Industry observers note that you can create the credential provider in the AgentCore console or with the AWS CLI. The private CA settings appear on the console only after you connect the OAuth client to a VPC, because private CA support applies only to private IdPs.

To create a credential provider that trusts your private CA (console).

The Root certificate authority field accepts either a root or an intermediate CA certificate.

Figure 2: Adding a root certificate from AWS Secrets Manager.

To create the same credential provider with the AWS CLI, add certificateConfigurations to the custom OAuth 2.0 provider configuration:.

Sources indicate that to use Amazon S3 instead, replace the certificateConfigurations entry with {"s3": {"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/trust-anchors/keycloak-root-ca.pem", "bucketOwnerAccountId": "444455556666"}}. If you leave out bucketOwnerAccountId, AgentCore Identity expects the bucket to be in your own account. To keep the client secret out of your shell history, you can reference a client secret that you store in Secrets Manager.

Recent findings suggest that agentCore Identity validates the certificate and sets up private connectivity in the background, so a new credential provider starts in the CREATING status. Check the status after a few minutes:.

On the console, the credential provider’s details page highlights the configured certificate under Root certificates. When the status is READY, your agents can request tokens from the IdP. If the status is CREATE_FAILED, the failureReason field explains why. For example, Leaf certificates are not allowed, must provide CA certificates only means that you uploaded the server certificate instead of the CA certificate. If you see Unable to access S3 object or Secrets Manager can't find the specified secret, check that the URI or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is correct. Also confirm that your identity can read the object or secret. If the provider is READY but token requests fail, confirm that the IdP’s server certificate was issued by the configured CA and has a SAN that matches the IdP hostname.

It has been revealed that after you verify that the credential provider trusts the private CA, monitor the CA certificate’s expiration and rotate it before it expires to prevent token request failures. AgentCore Identity publishes the EarliestCertificateDaysToExpiry metric to Amazon CloudWatch in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace when your agents request tokens through a credential provider that uses a private CA. The metric reports the days remaining until the earliest certificate in your PEM file expires. It has ProviderName, ProviderArn, and TokenVault dimensions. When you create an alarm, specify all three. We recommend a CloudWatch alarm that notifies you well before the value reaches zero, because token requests to the IdP stop working when the CA certificate expires.

In a recent development, NOTE: AgentCore Identity reads the certificate only when you create or revision the credential provider. If you change the secret or S3 object, call UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider afterward so that AgentCore Identity reads the new content. Include certificateConfigurations in the update request. If you leave it out, the credential provider stops trusting your private CA.

A PEM file can contain more than one CA certificate and AgentCore Identity trusts each of them. You can use this to rotate to a new CA while minimizing downtime:.

AgentCore Identity doesn’t check certificate revocation lists (CRLs) or use the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). This means that if an unauthorized party obtains the private key for an IdP server certificate, AgentCore Identity continues to trust that certificate. This trust lasts until the certificate expires or until you stop trusting the CA that issued it. To stop trusting a CA, remove it from the PEM file and update the credential provider.

A CA certificate contains no private key and is public by design, because you hand it to every client that has to trust your IdP. What you need to protect is the data integrity of the trust store, meaning the secret or S3 object that holds the certificate. If someone replaces the certificate or adds another CA certificate to the trust store, the next revision could let an unauthorized party who can redirect traffic impersonate your IdP.

Sources indicate that we recommend that you scope permissions around writes rather than reads. Give write access, such as s3:PutObject or secretsmanager:PutSecretValue, only to the team or pipeline that operates the IdP. Give read access to the principals that call CreateOauth2CredentialProvider or UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider. During these operations, AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate using the caller’s IAM permissions. The following bucket policy for a central identity account (444455556666) lets only the role that manages credential providers in a workload account (111122223333) read the CA certificates. It also requires that role to belong to your organization in AWS Organizations, and it denies writes from principals other than the IdP administrator role:.

The principal in the workload account also needs s3:GetObject in its own IAM policy. For Secrets Manager, which must be in the same account, use a resource-based policy on the secret to restrict writes to the IdP administrator role.

Because the secret is in the same account, IAM policies can grant read access, so the resource policy only needs to deny changes:.

Sources indicate that turn on S3 Versioning to recover an overwritten file and AWS CloudTrail data events to record each change. Because the CA certificate isn’t confidential, SSE-S3 encryption is sufficient and avoids the cross-account AWS KMS permissions that a customer managed key requires.

According to recent reports, keep the trust scope of each credential provider narrow. Upload only the CA that challenges your IdP’s server certificate, rather than your organization’s full trust bundle. If your IdPs use different CAs, store each CA certificate in its own secret or S3 object so that each credential provider trusts only the CA that it needs.

In a recent development, you can also use a private CA for inbound authorization. When AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a private IdP, it fetches the IdP’s discovery document and its signing keys from the JWKS endpoint. AgentCore Gateway validates the discovery URL when you create the gateway. If the CA certificate is missing or doesn’t match the IdP’s certificate chain, the gateway status changes to FAILED with the reason Failed to validate discovery url. To trust a private CA for that connection, add certificateConfigurations to the customJWTAuthorizer configuration, next to the existing privateEndpoint:.

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources that you created:.

In this post, we revealed how to connect AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a certificate from your own CA. You issued a server certificate with AWS Private CA, stored the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and referenced it from a credential provider. You also saw how to rotate the CA with a combined PEM file and how to limit who can change the certificate that your agents trust.

To learn more, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. For examples using Keycloak, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
  • Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
  • The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise looks include monthly credits for compute and inference.

Recent findings suggest that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Sources indicate that openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

Sources indicate that when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the fresh routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Industry observers note that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

According to recent reports, routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

It has been revealed that image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

Sources indicate that on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two newly introduced tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

Industry observers note that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

It has been revealed that requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

Design responsible AI controls for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A customer support chatbot that queries historical tickets and knowledge base articles stored in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition can deliver fast, context-aware answers.
  • In a recent development, amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition makes it more straightforward to operationalize responsible AI through its native Aurora Machine Learning (Aurora ML) capabilities.
  • Industry observers note that AWS defines eight core Responsible AI dimensions, published through the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and the Responsible Use of AI Guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A customer support chatbot that queries historical tickets and knowledge base articles stored in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition can deliver fast, context-aware answers. However, it also introduces challenges around privacy, accuracy, safety, and governance, especially when the underlying data contains sensitive customer information. In this post, we map the eight AWS Responsible AI (RAI) dimensions to Aurora PostgreSQL capabilities. We then walk through a design pattern for the Explainability dimension, using a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) based customer support chatbot as the reference use case. This post implements one dimension, Explainability, in depth. Treat it as Part 1 of a series rather than a full build-out of all eight.

In a recent development, amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition makes it more straightforward to operationalize responsible AI through its native Aurora Machine Learning (Aurora ML) capabilities. With Aurora ML, you can invoke Amazon SageMaker endpoints and Amazon Bedrock foundation models directly from SQL, without data movement, custom extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, or complex integrations. This post uses Aurora ML to generate vector embeddings from SQL, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer.

Industry observers note that AWS defines eight core Responsible AI dimensions, published through the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and the Responsible Use of AI Guide. These dimensions (Fairness, Explainability, Privacy and Security, Safety, Controllability, Veracity and Robustness, Governance, and Transparency) provide a structured framework for evaluating and implementing trustworthy AI systems.

It has been revealed that customer support systems often struggle to provide accurate, context-aware responses while maintaining privacy and compliance. Consider a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that uses RAG with pgvector embeddings, Amazon Bedrock model inference, and AWS Responsible AI guardrails to deliver grounded, explainable responses.

A customer can ask questions such as “Why was my last bill high?” or “Where is my last order?” and receive accurate answers with citations, while sensitive data remains obscured through personally identifiable information (PII) redaction and access controls.

In a recent development, the following table maps the eight AWS Responsible AI dimensions to practical implementation strategies for a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition. It highlights how database features, AWS AI services, and governance controls work together to deliver a trustworthy, secure, and explainable RAG-based chatbot.

Note: These are example approaches and may vary by use case.

This reference architecture shows how Responsible AI controls map to each component of a RAG-based chatbot on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition.

Industry observers note that an ingestion pipeline redacts PII from support tickets, FAQs, and product documents, then converts them into vector embeddings. When a user submits a query, AWS Lambda runs a semantic search over Aurora PostgreSQL, applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for privacy and grounding, sends the guarded context to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM), and logs every interaction for explainability and governance.

Lambda grounds responses in enterprise data, redacts PII and applies Row-Level Security (RLS) for privacy, records citations and interaction logs for explainability, and writes audit records for governance.

Industry observers note that when to build this versus use a managed service: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides built-in RAG with citations and is the simpler choice when default retrieval and citation behavior meets your needs. Build the custom logging design in this post when you need provenance stored in your own schema. That provenance includes retrieved versus cited sources, similarity scores, and guardrail traces that you can query with SQL and retain under your own policies.

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end architecture of this solution, showing the data ingestion flow (left), the query and response flow (center), and the responsible AI controls applied at each stage (center and right).

Figure 1: Architecture of RAG-based customer support chatbot with Responsible AI controls on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.

An ingestion pipeline loads historical support tickets, FAQs, and product documentation into Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL after redacting PII, using the pgvector and aws_ml extensions for vector operations and Aurora ML integration.

The Aurora ML aws_bedrock.invoke_model_get_embeddings function transforms the text into Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors (1,024 dimensions), and pgvector stores them.

Aurora PostgreSQL functions as both a relational store for structured customer data and a vector database for semantic search.

This section presents the database-layer design patterns that make every AI-generated response traceable, from the user query, through retrieval and guardrail evaluation, to the final answer and its citations.

Create the core tables for customer data, chat sessions, interaction logging, and feedback:.

It has been revealed that start by creating the schema and the tables you need. Each table serves a specific Responsible AI dimension:.

The customers table stores profiles for tenant-aware access control:.

It has been revealed that the chat_interactions table is the core of the Explainability implementation. It logs every query-response cycle with full RAG provenance, including retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, cited versus retrieved sources, guardrail traces, and the model used:.

Because chat_interactions stores raw request_text and response_text, protect it the same way as the source data: redact PII before the INSERT (reusing the ingestion-time guardrail), or encrypt those columns with pgcrypto, and apply Row-Level Security to the log tables so tenants cannot read each other’s interactions. Logging unprotected customer content would undercut the Privacy and Security control this design is meant to demonstrate.

The chat_feedback table captures user ratings and comments on chatbot responses, which supports the Controllability dimension. The ON DELETE CASCADE clause makes sure the 90-day retention purge does not fail with foreign key violations:.

Create the retrieval layer with vector embeddings, tenant isolation, and Aurora ML integration:.

Create an HNSW index for fast approximate nearest neighbor search:.

Enforce tenant isolation with Row-Level Security so that vector search results are scoped to the current tenant before data leaves the database:.

Generate vector embeddings directly from SQL using Aurora ML, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer:.

Always redact PII before inserting data into the knowledge base. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (the ApplyGuardrail API) or Amazon Comprehend (the detect_pii_entities API) to identify and mask PII in your ingestion pipeline, as shown in the following example:.

In a recent development, when a query reaches your application layer, retrieve the top matching knowledge chunks using the pgvector cosine similarity operator. The following SQL query indicates this pattern:.

Note: The 0.7 cosine-similarity cutoff drops weakly related chunks so the model is not grounded on noise. Tune it against your own data. The category filter and this threshold both post-filter HNSW results and may return fewer than 5 rows. Raise hnsw.ef_search or use iterative index scans (pgvector 0.8.0+) to compensate.

Industry observers note that the following pseudocode reveals the key patterns for contextual grounding, guardrail-intervention handling, citation parsing, and interaction logging. The snippets focus on the Responsible AI logic rather than application plumbing.

Use guardContent blocks to enable contextual grounding in the Bedrock Converse API:.

Check stopReason to handle cases where the guardrail blocks the response:.

Recent findings suggest that distinguish actually cited sources from all retrieved sources. On an Explainability post, this distinction is the point:.

In a recent development, log every interaction for Explainability. The INSERT captures the full RAG provenance chain:.

Industry observers note that we define confidence_score as the mean cosine similarity of the top-k retrieved chunks. The intent field classifies the query (for example, billing or order_status), and response_latency_ms records end-to-end inference time.

Every chatbot interaction (the user query, retrieved chunks, similarity scores, response, and citations) is logged to the chat_interactions table using the INSERT shown in Step 3, supporting Explainability and Transparency. Customer feedback captured in chat_feedback supports continuous improvement, reinforcing Controllability. For Governance, pgaudit provides query audit trails, and pg_cron drives automated data retention.

Set up pgaudit and pg_cron, which both require shared_preload_libraries (see Prerequisites):.

Archive both tables to Amazon S3 and purge only after the export succeeds. Running archive and purge as two independent cron jobs is unsafe: if the archive fails, a separately scheduled purge still deletes the rows. Wrap both in one function so the DELETE runs only when the export returns. Also archive chat_feedback, because the cascade would otherwise delete feedback that was not saved. The 90-day window matches a typical support-data retention policy. Adjust it to your own regulatory requirements.

Industry observers note that run one question end to end, then read the row it produced. That single row is the evidence the design works: it shows which chunks were retrieved, how similar they were, which sources the answer actually cited, and the guardrail outcome.

In a recent development, expected: One row whose cited_sources is a subset of retrieved_chunk_ids, similarity_scores at or above your 0.7 threshold, and a guardrail_action of NONE for a clean question. If cited_sources is empty, the model did not ground its answer and the response should be treated with caution.

Industry observers note that amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, with pgvector, Row-Level Security, pgaudit, pgcrypto, pg_cron, and Aurora ML, provides database-layer building blocks for Responsible AI. Several dimensions also depend on AWS services outside the database, as the mapping table reveals.

In this post, we focused on the Explainability dimension as a detailed design walkthrough. By logging retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, cited sources, and guardrail traces in Aurora, you get a queryable audit trail at the database layer. The mapping table shows how the remaining dimensions build on the same foundation, combining Aurora PostgreSQL features with AWS AI services.

In a recent development, view CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released fresh versions for several affected products and recommends to upgrade to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Industry observers note that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

In a recent development, I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

In a recent development, my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

It has been revealed that strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

In a recent development, before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Sources indicate that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

Sources indicate that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Sources indicate that strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

In a recent development, all of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

It has been revealed that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization proposal of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

In a recent development, the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Sources indicate that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

It has been revealed that most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It has been revealed that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

It has been revealed that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Sources indicate that beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

According to recent reports, finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers, who have achieved a machine in the middle position, to relay NTLM authentication and impersonate a legitimate user. Recommended Practices CISA recommends customers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. #2311. How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2473 w)

How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure.
  • As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost.
  • In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS.

As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks.

In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend.

In a recent development, at Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models.

Recent findings suggest that each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task.

After a rollout, observability reveals us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why.

You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch:.

On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model.

Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock.

Figure 1 shows how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings.

According to recent reports, figure 1: Coding agents and cloud agents call Amazon Bedrock through our LLM gateway. Our usage records and CloudWatch metrics show real use, and we use eval results to set defaults and effort ceilings.

The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change.

Industry observers note that tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs.

You also need three things of your own:.

Sources indicate that before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements.

Recent findings suggest that start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend.

A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task.

Bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts.

Reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces.

Sources indicate that on the afternoon a new model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org.

Recent findings suggest that that speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work:.

Sources indicate that the grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config:.

Both examples use the formats of Harbor, an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out.

In a recent development, running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3.

Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone.

Recent findings suggest that when latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: TimeToFirstToken for the wait before generation starts, OutputTokenCount for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes:.

In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard.

Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A fresh model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task.

One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model. We rolled it out, capped effort at high, and asked people to use low or medium for most work.

It has been revealed that A few weeks after launch, we priced model A’s production usage at list price and looked at it in aggregate. Average weekly spend per user was several times higher on model A than on the model before it. Each model A request cost about three times as much, and the average model A user sent about three times as many requests.

In a recent development, output tokens made up only a tenth of a request’s cost. Most of the cost went to cached context, which the model re-read on every request. Model A could work on its own for a long time, so people started long, self-directed sessions with it.

In a recent development, the eval measured the model on a task. Production measured how people chose to work with it.

Recent findings suggest that later, a newer model scored higher than model A on the same tasks and grader, at about a sixth of its cost per task. We moved model A’s consumers to it with a configuration change.

Recent findings suggest that we then checked the change in aggregate on the same user group, the heavy users of model A. In their first full week on the newer model, the group sent about the same number of requests to their main model, and the group’s spend on that model fell to about a seventh.

According to recent reports, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, Bedrock checks your tokens-per-minute quota when a request arrives, before the model writes anything. It reserves your uncached input tokens and your cache writes, plus max_tokens, the most output the request is allowed. It adjusts that reservation as the model generates and returns the unused part when the request settles. Cache reads never count against the quota, so a request can be cheap against your quota and expensive on your bill. Output tokens settle at a burndown rate that is 1:1 on most models and several times that on some current models, so check your model’s rate.

According to recent reports, A dashboard of billed tokens can show room while requests are being throttled. In our session’s example, the quota was 1 million tokens per minute and traffic was 300 requests per minute. The dashboard showed about 30 percent of quota. After applying a 5:1 output-token burndown rate, completed requests consumed about 77 percent.

Admission uses a different calculation. Each request initially reserved 600 uncached input tokens plus a max_tokens of 4,096, for a total of 4,696 tokens. Responses were about 800 tokens at p99.

Lowering max_tokens to 1,024 cut the initial reservation to 1,624 tokens, about 65 percent smaller. The limit was still above p99. For unchanged input and output, final quota consumption stays the same. The smaller reservation leaves more room to admit requests. Monitor stopReason to catch truncated responses. Use backoff and jitter, and cap retries.

In a recent development, demand can also outrun the headroom you have on any one model. You want to know where work can go before you need it, and our evals answer that. The answer can be a model from another model family. For every major model we use, we keep at least one equivalent that performs as well on our evals and that we can load-balance to. Without those evals, choosing where the work goes would be guesswork.

It has been revealed that if headroom on a model stays tight, we can rebalance by changing a default in our configuration. First check that the equivalent model has capacity for the extra load and that your quota covers it. Keep enough traffic on it to hold your access, too: after a model enters its Legacy period, existing customers can lose access after 15 days of inactivity. A Legacy model works until end-of-life, and after that Bedrock removes it from every Region, requests to it fail, and Bedrock doesn’t move your traffic automatically. Alarm when LegacyModelInvocations rises above zero.

Bedrock runtime metrics are dimensioned by ModelId, so you can see which model served a request but not which team sent it. Bedrock publishes these metrics both with and without the ModelId dimension, and a request that fails before Bedrock resolves the model appears only in the series without it, so filtering by ModelId undercounts errors. Bedrock offers three ways to attribute spend:.

Behind a gateway, Bedrock sees the gateway’s role, so have the gateway assume a role for each user with its own RoleSessionName or session tags. Cache those credentials for the session, because assuming a role on every request can exceed your AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) rate quotas. Requests keep succeeding when attribution breaks, so set an alarm for when Bedrock fails to deliver invocation logs.

Our usage records let us attribute usage by model, client, team and user, which we use only in aggregate for cost and capacity planning. We compute cost per task from the same four token counts, so we can compare token mix and cost between our evals and production.

We can go from a model release to a deployment decision overnight. After one rollout, average weekly spend per user on model A was several times that on the previous model. We moved its heavy users to a newer model. In their first full week, the group’s spend on its main model fell to about a seventh, with roughly the same number of requests. For every major model we use, our evals identify an equivalent we can rebalance to.

Recent findings suggest that after testing, stop the eval jobs and agent processes you started. If you enabled model invocation logging only for this walkthrough, disable it in each Region using DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration.

According to recent reports, after callers no longer use them, delete the application inference profiles you created using DeleteInferenceProfile. Remove IAM roles, policies, and resource tags created only for this walkthrough. Deactivate cost allocation tags used only for these tests. Delete test CloudWatch log groups and S3 log objects you no longer need.

We run four checks every time a model ships:.

We chose Amazon Bedrock for access to multiple model families through one API. It lets us use our existing AWS access controls and logging while AWS manages the model infrastructure. We use evals to choose models for our work and observability to know when those choices need another look.

Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Upcoming Frontier and Use Cases

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • According to recent reports, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

According to recent reports, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

Industry observers note that IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Industry observers note that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to upcoming series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

It has been revealed that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Industry observers note that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

In a recent development, the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

In a recent development, A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Sources indicate that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

In a recent development, -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

Sources indicate that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

According to recent reports, -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

According to recent reports, figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

Recent findings suggest that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

In a recent development, to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

According to recent reports, when the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

Industry observers note that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

According to recent reports, figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

Industry observers note that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

According to recent reports, figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as fresh sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

It has been revealed that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

Industry observers note that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

In a recent development, the bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

Industry observers note that on each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

Industry observers note that if a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

Recent findings suggest that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

According to recent reports, figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Recent findings suggest that figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Recent findings suggest that view CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Please also have a look on following Software Field Bulletins: Teamcenter: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869204 Polarion: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869197 Manufacturing Operations Center (Opcenter) and Process Preparation X: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869211 Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.
